description: A third-year student with a strong background in high-level Python development and theoretical computer science who is apprehensive about the transition to low-level C programming.

nodes.personalizationRationale: This node provides critical programming foundations for a student in the no_prior_exposure tier to ensure they can follow later implementation examples.
nodes.title: Systems Programming Bridge: Intro to C
nodes.description: A foundational introduction to C syntax, pointers, and memory management specifically tailored for systems programming tasks.

nodes.title: Hardware Foundations for OS
nodes.personalizationRationale: For a student with no_prior_exposure, bridging the gap between hardware and software is necessary before discussing kernel operations.
nodes.description: Visualizing how hardware interacts with software, including interrupts, registers, and the fetch-execute cycle.
Clarifying the distinction between privileged and non-privileged instructions and how the CPU switches between them.
nodes.title: The Kernel vs. User Mode Divide
nodes.personalizationRationale: Establishing the concept of protection early is vital for students in the no_prior_exposure tier to understand why OS kernels exist.

nodes.description: Overview of OS services, system calls, and the various organizational structures (monolithic vs microkernel).
nodes.title: Operating System Structures & Services
nodes.personalizationRationale: Standard core content covering the fundamental architecture of modern operating systems.
Given the student's no_prior_exposure status, this node builds the process abstraction necessary for all subsequent learning.
nodes.title: Process Lifecycle and Operations
nodes.description: Understanding the Process Control Block (PCB), states (Running, Waiting, Ready), and the fork/exec model.
Comparative study of shared memory versus message passing and an introduction to sockets for communication.
nodes.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) Fundamentals
nodes.personalizationRationale: Essential core concepts for understanding how independent processes coordinate in a single system.

nodes.title: Threads and Multithreading Models
nodes.personalizationRationale: Transitioning from processes to threads is a core requirement for modern systems development.
nodes.description: Exploring multithreading libraries, thread-local storage, and the relationship between user and kernel threads.
Analyzing FCFS, SJF, Priority, and Round Robin scheduling algorithms and their performance metrics.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core analytical component required for modeling OS behavior and resource management.
nodes.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms and Criteria

nodes.description: A comprehensive review of Chapters 1-5 content including process management, threads, and basic scheduling in preparation for the midterm.
nodes.title: Midterm Review: Foundations and Scheduling
nodes.personalizationRationale: Mandatory midterm checkpoint to ensure a student with no_prior_exposure has mastered the foundational half of the course.

nodes.description: Defining race conditions, critical sections, and the implementation of Mutex locks and Semaphores.
nodes.title: Process Synchronization and Mutexes
nodes.personalizationRationale: Synchronization is a difficult but mandatory core topic that requires careful build-up for students with no prior systems exposure.
Standard classic problems that every student must master for the final exam and project deliveries.
nodes.title: Classic Synchronization Problems
nodes.description: Exploring the Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, and Dining Philosophers problems using monitors and semaphores.
Techniques for deadlock characterization, prevention via resource ordering, and avoidance via the Banker's Algorithm.
nodes.title: Deadlock Detection and Avoidance
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core material on system stability and resource safety, scaled appropriately to the block's smaller lesson count.

nodes.description: Physical memory allocation, contiguous versus non-contiguous allocation, and the basics of hardware paging.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Crucial core knowledge for understanding how the OS manages limited physical hardware resources.
nodes.title: Main Memory and Paging Structures
Virtual Memory and Page Replacement
nodes.personalizationRationale: Complex core material that is heavily tested and required for the final project on memory management.
nodes.description: Demand paging, page replacement algorithms (LRU, FIFO, Optimal), and the mechanics of thrashing.
The I/O hardware-software interface, device drivers, and techniques for improving I/O performance.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core requirement for understanding the communication between the CPU and external peripherals.
nodes.title: I/O Systems and Performance

nodes.description: Directory structures, file allocation methods (indexed, linked), and free-space management.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Foundational storage concepts required for the final exam and understanding persistent data.
nodes.title: File System Implementation

nodes.description: Cumulative review of all blocks from OS foundations through file systems to prepare for the 40% final exam.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Mandatory cumulative assessment checkpoint to ensure the student with no_prior_exposure has achieved full course objectives.
nodes.title: Cumulative Final Exam Review
